title: Brass bands and playing on a parade truck in 1957
summary: A band truck out of the Ninth Ward with Justin Adams on amplified guitar, white clubs he played for, and a brass band he cannot name.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Did you hear any brass bands on a carnival day? Well yeah, well you know, what happened, you would always hear some, there'll always be some

little marching club with a brass band. And I'm talking about blacks. There was always a band coming along the street, somebody playing, you really don't know who they are. But there's always a, you would always hear marching band. Now, Herman Sherman, you remember Herman Sherman? No, he died. He died. But he was one of these that was always in somebody's marching band. Now I remember one year, and this was either 1950, it had to be 57, we played on a truck, my whole original Untouchable band, we played on a truck, one of these big trailer trucks, one of these clubs from down in St. Bernard. They hired my band to play. And they said we had the best truck that year. But because of the band, see what happened with the guitar, and it was the first time I had heard it, because I didn't know about that converter that a guitar could hook to the battery and get electricity for his amp.
Yeah.
And Justin Allen was the guitar one of the best rhythm and blues guitar players that, and boy, we just lit up Canal Street and Ramport Street that year. But it had to be 1957.
So you all played on the truck?
On the truck, yeah. As it moved? As it moved, right.
Which parade was this?
I can't remember. I know it came from, it came from the 9th Ward. It came from the 9th Ward.
It started in the 9th Ward?

Uh huh. Came up. Came up, yeah. To Canal Street? Yeah, came up to Canal Street, and went, and then we went back down, we went back down Ramport Street. But, and we played from about 10 o'clock to 5 o'clock that evening, but it was hard. We had some fun. And it didn't make no whole lot of money either. Never was a whole lot of money, but it was so much fun. And you know, that's part of recognition. You know, there was a white organization I used to play for, the Pink Elephants. I don't know if you ever heard of Pink Elephants. I don't know if you ever heard of Pink Elephants. No. I don't know. Okay. Mike Ginnard. He's a big man in the fire department, in the union, in the New Orleans Fire. But Mike was one of the members of the Pink Elephants. I used to play for them quite a bit. But that was one of the white clubs I played for. I played for the lucky 69ers. Oh, I got a whole guy. I see all of them talking about now. I got all of these books in here. Who I played for? You know, I got to have my books from 1957 up to right now. Everywhere I played. Who I played for. LSU, Ole Miss, Mississippi, Northeastern, Southwestern. I got all that right there. We'll talk about that. But specifically, did you ever go to any funerals or funerals? Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. You played singles?
Yeah. Do you know who the brass band was? Who was it?
I remember Earl Anderson was a trumpet player. I know Joe Tillman was a saxophone player. And that's all I can remember.
A bass drummer? Yeah, bass.
I can't remember who it was. I can't remember who that was. It had to be about seven, eight piece bands. But we played all day.
It was a parade. Yeah, in Lutton, Louisiana.
I'm sure it was.
